questions.question_text: In South Dakota, a single agent represents:
questions.correct_answer: Only one party with full fiduciary duties
distractors: Both parties with limited disclosure
Neither party as a neutral facilitator
One party with reduced obligations
questions.explanation: A single agent represents only one party to the transaction and owes that client the full duties of reasonable skill and care, good faith, loyalty, and fidelity (SDCL 36-21A-1(18), 36-21A-132).

questions.question_text: A limited agent in South Dakota represents both buyer and seller. What consent is required?
questions.correct_answer: Informed written consent from both parties
distractors: Verbal consent from the buyer only
Written consent from the seller only
No special consent beyond standard disclosure
questions.explanation: A limited agent may act only with the informed written consent of all parties (SDCL 36-21A-140). The limited agent may not reveal that a buyer would pay more, that a seller would take less, either party's motives, or their flexibility on financing.

questions.question_text: Which duty does a South Dakota licensee owe to ALL clients regardless of agency type?
questions.correct_answer: Present all written offers in a timely manner
distractors: Negotiate the lowest possible price for the buyer
Share the other party's financial information
Recommend a specific lender or inspector
questions.explanation: Every client relationship — single agent, limited agent, or subagent — carries the duty to present all written offers in a timely manner, even while the property is already under contract (SDCL 36-21A-132, 36-21A-140).

questions.question_text: A licensee discovers a material defect in a listed property. Under SD agency law, what must they do?
questions.correct_answer: Disclose the adverse material fact to all parties
distractors: Disclose only if the buyer specifically asks
Keep it confidential as the seller's agent
Report it to the SDREC before disclosure
questions.explanation: Adverse material facts known to the licensee must be disclosed to clients and customers alike (SDCL 36-21A-132, 36-21A-134). They include material defects in the property, title defects expected to survive closing, and required environmental disclosures.

questions.question_text: Which obligation is specifically listed among a SD agent's duties to clients?
questions.correct_answer: Advise clients to seek expert advice when needed
distractors: Guarantee the property will appreciate in value
Provide legal opinions on contract disputes
Determine the exact market value of property
questions.explanation: Licensees must advise clients to get expert advice on material matters beyond their own expertise (SDCL 36-21A-132). Legal, tax, structural, and environmental questions belong to the professionals in those fields, not to the agent.

questions.question_text: When must a South Dakota licensee provide the Real Estate Relationships Disclosure form?
distractors: At the time of contract signing
Within 48 hours of the first showing
Only when requested by the client
questions.explanation: The written relationships disclosure is due at first substantive contact with a seller or buyer who has not already signed with a broker (SDCL 36-21A-147). If the consumer refuses to sign it, the licensee notes that on the copy and keeps it.

questions.question_text: A licensee begins discussing a buyer's pre-approval amount and ideal price range. This conversation qualifies as:
distractors: A casual conversation with no obligations
A protected negotiation under attorney privilege
A marketing discussion requiring no disclosure
questions.explanation: Substantive contact begins once the conversation moves past informational basics into the buyer's specific financial qualifications (SDCL 36-21A-129). Pre-approval amounts and a target price range are exactly that, so the relationships disclosure is due.

questions.question_text: The Real Estate Relationships Disclosure form in South Dakota is:
questions.correct_answer: Neither a contract nor an addendum
distractors: A binding agency contract with the licensee
An addendum to the purchase agreement
A mandatory listing agreement supplement
questions.explanation: The disclosure is informational — it explains the relationships the broker offers, and a customer's signature acknowledging receipt is not a contract with the licensee (SDCL 36-21A-147). A separate written agreement still has to create the relationship.

questions.question_text: In South Dakota, how is a brokerage relationship with a buyer created?
distractors: By a verbal agreement once the licensee shows a property
Automatically after three property showings
By the buyer signing the relationships disclosure form
questions.explanation: No brokerage relationship arises by word or action alone — only a written agreement creates one (SDCL 36-21A-1(24)). A licensee may still answer questions or give a one-time showing of one property without forming any relationship.

questions.question_text: A buyer asks their buyer's agent whether a registered sex offender lives near the property. What must the licensee do?
questions.correct_answer: Disclose any actual knowledge the licensee has
distractors: Decline to answer — the information is confidential
Investigate the registry and report the findings
Refer the question to the seller's agent
questions.explanation: A buyer's agent has no duty to investigate or volunteer sex offender information but must disclose actual knowledge when the client asks (SDCL 36-21A-138.1). A licensee representing the seller owes no such duty at all (SDCL 36-21A-134.1).

questions.question_text: In South Dakota, an appointed agent provides what level of representation?
questions.correct_answer: Full representation to their assigned client
distractors: Limited representation to both parties equally
No representation as a neutral facilitator
Partial representation with reduced duties
questions.explanation: An appointed agent gives one client full representation to the exclusion of the brokerage's other licensees, and the appointment must be in writing (SDCL 36-21A-141.1). Making the appointment does not turn the responsible broker into a limited agent.

questions.question_text: A transaction broker in South Dakota may NOT do which of the following?
questions.correct_answer: Advise to the detriment of any party
distractors: Assist with completing transaction forms
Provide market data and property information
Help coordinate inspections and appraisals
questions.explanation: A transaction broker assists without being an agent or advocate and may never advise any party to another party's detriment (SDCL 36-21A-144). Presenting offers, accounting for funds, and disclosing adverse material facts are still required.

questions.question_text: Two licensees in the same brokerage each represent opposing sides of a transaction. This arrangement is BEST described as:
distractors: Single agency for both parties
Transaction brokerage by default
An illegal conflict of interest
questions.explanation: The responsible broker may appoint each licensee to represent one side, giving both clients full representation instead of limited agency (SDCL 36-21A-141.1). If a single licensee ends up representing both sides, that licensee becomes a limited agent.

questions.question_text: Under the 2024 NAR settlement rules, what must buyers in South Dakota sign before beginning home tours?
questions.correct_answer: A written buyer-broker agreement specifying the fee
distractors: A disclosure that the seller pays commission
A waiver of their right to representation
An acknowledgment of the listing agent's duties
questions.explanation: Under the 2024 NAR settlement, MLS participants must have a signed written buyer agreement stating the agent's compensation before touring a home. It is an MLS policy requirement rather than South Dakota statute, and the amount stays negotiable.

questions.question_text: Parties working with a transaction broker in South Dakota are classified as:
distractors: Clients with full fiduciary protection
Principals under the agency agreement
Third parties with no relationship
questions.explanation: A transaction broker's parties are customers, not clients (SDCL 36-21A-144). They get reasonable skill and care, timely presentation of offers, an accounting, and disclosure of adverse material facts — but no loyalty or advocacy.
